chunks: Luu 1 Thien Luu Prof. Bains CRWT 2301 March 30th, 2026 New Independence Poem 1: Parents love Love at home doesn’t need to be heard. It wakes up early, making sure I don’t go hungry It’s my favorite smell. The smell of garlic frying on a stove, a comforting yet rich aroma outside my bedroom door. Love washes the dishes even after a long day of work, even when they didn’t make them dirty. It folds my laundry, irons my wrinkled clothes with care, like it does with me When I ask to go out, to play longer with some friends, to be free in the silent night, love does not stop me. Luu 2 It whispers through the phone, Don’t get lost. Stay safe. Enjoy yourself. Love doesn’t have to be through the mouth. always shouting my name from across the house, asking for assistance or just checking in, their voices echoing through every room. Next to my room was my sister, whose constant calls with her friends would bleed through the insulation- a reminder that the house was full. The lights were always on. The living room was constantly glowing, the kitchen staying bright just in case. That yellow light shined across the house, spilling a cozy, comfortable feeling into every corner, making sure nothing ever went gloomy. But my new home is different. The living room stays empty– a black box waiting for me to flip the switch to wake it up. Everything is very quiet. All I can hear is the AC– the constant buzzing of a machine rather than my family. Luu 4 I fall back onto my bed and stare at the ceiling. Instead of that yellow, cozy glow, the light above me is sharp and white like a blank page, marking my new start. . Instead of that yellow, cozy glow, the light above me is sharp and white like a blank page, marking my new start. Luu 5 Poem 3: Family of One My body remembers by instinct. I grab a cart, steer it from the back, and head straight to the vegetable aisle at my new local H-E-B. I reach for the big box of baby spinach. “Organic,” I remember my mom always telling me, and then the slab of salmon– the long orange curve meant to feed four. I didn’t even stop to think that the meal was only meant to serve one person now. In the dairy aisle, my hand reaches for two: whole milk for me, and almond for my sister. I don’t realize my mistake until I looked back at the cart and realized I was steering alone. No sister behind me to take the second gallon, just the cold air of the aisle. Twenty-four large brown eggs. The amount I would always get for us. But now, I cut the count down to twelve, shrinking the carton just for myself. brown eggs. The amount I would always get for us. But now, I cut the count down to twelve, shrinking the carton just for myself. Luu 6 I stand in the spice aisle, trying to remember which bottle they usually get. I grab the one with the familiar label, the one I thought made me remember home cooking. Dinner tonight was like a stranger, the salmon didn’t taste the same. The spinach tasted so foreign. I had bought the wrong seasoning. Luu 7 Poem 4: Learning They grew slowly a yellow stain around the edges, small enough to ignore until I can’t. It always appeared for a bit and somehow disappeared before I noticed it growing. Instead of my mother, now I stand here. A bottle of bleach on my left, an old towel on my right. Reading the instructions for something I should already know. Did I spray enough? When do I wipe? y enough? When do I wipe? I could not tell. The floor here is different. Back home, everything was wood– easy to clean, smooth to walk on, making sound upon every step, letting me know someone else was there. Luu 8 Now the carpet holds everything: crumbs, dust, and even footsteps. I vacuumed back and forth, hoping it would pick up everything, especially the ones I can’t see. I lost power one week after moving in. Just my room. Everything else was the same, like nothing happened. I sat there, waiting, hoping someone would notice, hoping someone would fix it. But no one came. I opened a box in the wall, looked at the many switches, wondering what to do. I flipped one. The living room went dark. I flipped another, until my room went bright again. It was that simple. Luu 9 Poem 5: New Home I moved my bed twice until it felt right. I brought a pillow from my old room that fits my head just like before. oved my bed twice until it felt right. I brought a pillow from my old room that fits my head just like before. A brand-new bed, similar to the one I left behind, makes the room smaller, makes the room cozier, makes the room mine. I set out my toothbrush, my soap, my shampoo– all familiar, all the same as home. I now shop with a plan, I cook my own way. The fridge now holds more than just ingredients; it holds new habits, new memories, and a new smell. Luu 10 I chat with hometown friend, just like before. Our conversation fills the silence that once made me restless. I often call my parents, talking about something, about anything. I still feel their worries, their care, giving me a sense of comfort. I clean better, organize better, and live more independently. This place is mine. I’m adjusting to this new home.
